read.sections.0.text.note: 'Học hỏi tập thể' for 'collective learning' is my choice (not in KEY_TERMS). Alternatives: 'học tập tập thể', 'sự học hỏi chung'. 'Tạo hình dụng cụ bằng đá' for 'shape a stone tool'.
read.sections.0.text.source: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, improve it and then teach it to others. In this way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little and pass it on, so it is not lost when one person stops using it.
read.sections.0.text.back: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, make it better, then teach it to others. That way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person finds a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little and pass it on, so it is not lost when one person stops using it.

A child learns a skill from an older person. Then the child makes it better. Later, the child teaches others. So knowledge grows from one generation to the next. This is called collective learning. read.sections.0.simpler.back: Many animals can learn. Some even use tools. But humans are very good at sharing what they learn. We use speech to explain ideas. read.sections.1.heading.back: Clues from places where early people lived

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Nhà khảo cổ học' (archaeologist), 'hang Blombos' (Blombos Cave, name kept), 'mảnh đá đỏ' for the red ochre rock. A reviewer might prefer 'đá son' or 'đất son'. 75.000 năm kept.
read.sections.1.text.source: Early humans did not leave any written records, so how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things that people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, fireplaces and art. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked. Art shows that people used signs and symbols. In Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone cut a neat pattern into a piece of red rock about 75,000 years ago. However, one object rarely proves a whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.
read.sections.1.text.back: Early people left no written records, so how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things people left behind, like tools, bones, footprints, hearths and art. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burnt seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked. Art shows that people used signs and symbols. In Blombos Cave in South Africa, about 75,000 years ago, someone engraved a neat pattern on a piece of red stone. However, one object rarely proves a whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Early humans did not write. So how do we learn about them? An archaeologist studies things that people left behind. Tools, bones and art are all clues. A worn tool shows how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth show what people cooked. In South Africa, people marked a red rock with lines. That was about 75,000 years ago. But one object does not tell the whole story. So archaeologists look at many finds.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Early people did not write. So how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things people of long ago left. Tools, bones and art are all clues. A worn tool shows how people used it. Burnt seeds in a hearth show what people cooked. In South Africa, people long ago engraved lines on a piece of red stone. That happened about 75,000 years ago. But one object does not tell the whole story. So archaeologists look at many finds.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Moving and adapting to new places
read.sections.2.heading.back: Moving and adapting to new places

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Loài người chúng ta' for 'our species' (Homo sapiens). 'Lan sang' for spread. 'Úc', 'châu Mỹ' as the usual names. Check 'thích nghi' fits as 'adapt'.
read.sections.2.text.source: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over many thousands of years, groups slowly spread into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long trip. It happened a little at a time, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, and they made new tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. A tool may look simple, but making it took planning, skill and teaching.
read.sections.2.text.back: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over many thousands of years, groups slowly spread to Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long journey. It happened little by little, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, then made new tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. A tool may look simple, but making it needs planning, skill and ways of teaching each other.

write.example.source: The clues suggest that early humans learned skills from each other. Clue 4 shows tools with the same shape at sites far apart. This may mean that people copied a good design and taught it to others. Another clue is the hearth with layers of ash. People may have used the same fireplace many times and shared what they knew about fire and food. Together, these clues suggest collective learning. But the clues cannot tell us what words people used or who made the first tool.

watch.summary.source: This video explains collective learning. Humans can use language to share ideas in great detail. So one person does not have to learn everything alone. Each generation can learn what older people knew and then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelter. This helped groups adapt to many different places, from hot lands to cold ones. We cannot hear what early people said. But tools slowly got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning did not make every group the same. Each community used what it knew in its own way, to fit its own place.
watch.summary.back: This video explains collective learning. People can use language to share ideas in great detail. So one person does not have to learn everything alone. Each generation can learn what older people know, then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early people shared how to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelter. This helped groups adapt to many different places, from hot regions to cold ones. We cannot hear what people of long ago said. But tools gradually got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning does not make every group identical. Each community uses what it knows in its own way, to suit the place it lives.
